notes.purpose: A three-segment arm with a two-finger parallel gripper, declared in the same schema as the humanoid hand. It is here to test whether the architecture is about grasping or about THIS hand. Nothing above the solvers should have to change: the same metric names, the same primitives, the same refusals, the same phase sequence.
notes.what_is_different: Almost everything below the interface. Four joints instead of a shoulder chain and nineteen finger bones. Fingers that translate rather than curl, so there is no thumb, no opposition to arrange, no curl to lock, and the C-shape the humanoid had to be taught is the gripper's resting geometry. If the same controller drives both, the vocabulary was the right abstraction.
notes.what_is_the_same: The numbers. palm_to_object_m is the distance from whatever does the holding to the object's surface, whether that is a palm pad or the plate between two fingers. object_in_grasp_m is the object's distance from the line between the gripping surfaces. Both are properties of grasping, not of hands.
notes.amplitude: Declared per primitive here as it is for the hand, and for the same reason: a number between 0 and 1 does not describe itself, and four failures in this project came from assuming the wrong meaning.

base.note: on a pedestal 34 cm above the table and 60 cm back. Mounted flat ON the surface the arm could not reach forward without swinging a link under it, so every legal pose was a useless one: it stayed above the table and stopped reaching. Real arms stand on a plinth for the same reason.

joints.name: finger_left
joints.note: Travel starts at the pad half-thickness plus clearance, which is the physically right bound: at zero the pads pass straight through each other. Each pad is 24 mm thick and the two geoms do not collide (their contype/conaffinity masks exclude the pair), so the jaws could drive 12 mm of pure interpenetration before they were even nominally shut -- and opening() reports max(0, centres - 24 mm), so it read 0.00 cm through all of it. That is what made the fingers appear to phase into the block. The floor of 0.0155 m leaves 7.0 mm of daylight at full closure. Maximum aperture is unchanged at 86 mm, since only the lower bound moved.

joints.name: finger_right
joints.note: Travel starts at the pad half-thickness plus clearance, which is the physically right bound: at zero the pads pass straight through each other. Each pad is 24 mm thick and the two geoms do not collide (their contype/conaffinity masks exclude the pair), so the jaws could drive 12 mm of pure interpenetration before they were even nominally shut -- and opening() reports max(0, centres - 24 mm), so it read 0.00 cm through all of it. That is what made the fingers appear to phase into the block. The floor of 0.0155 m leaves 7.0 mm of daylight at full closure. Maximum aperture is unchanged at 86 mm, since only the lower bound moved.

kinematics.support_note: The surface the arm is bolted to and works above. No link may go below it: the joint ranges alone do not say so, and the solver drove the first elbow to 30 cm under the table, which reads on screen as an arm rising out of the floor. A range of motion is not the same as a reachable workspace.

primitives.name: move_to
primitives.amplitude: fraction of the way to the target
primitives.describes: carry the gripper to a face of the object and arrive square to it, with the object between the fingers rather than beyond them
refuses_when: either finger carries more than 2.5 N -- the gripper is already touching, and the arm has more leverage than the fingers
the gripper is holding the object -- the face being approached is between the fingers, so approaching drives the gripper through what it carries
the object is moving faster than 0.02 m/s -- that is the approach pushing it, and force does not register it

primitives.name: open_grip
primitives.amplitude: how far toward the open shape, not how wide
primitives.describes: open the fingers to the object's width plus clearance, so it can enter the opening
refuses_when: the gripper is holding the object -- opening is how you put it down

primitives.name: close_grip
primitives.amplitude: the contact force to close TO, in newtons, low arriving and high carrying
primitives.describes: bring the fingers together onto the object
refuses_when: the object is too far off the line between the finger pads -- closing could only push it
the opening is already at the object's own width -- solids do not compress

primitives.name: segment_1
primitives.amplitude: a RATE of rise, re-run every frame, not a height
refuses_when: the grip carries less than the object's weight with margin -- it squeezes instead

primitives.name: carry_over
primitives.amplitude: fraction of the way to the target
primitives.describes: carry what is held to a point above the bin, high enough to clear its rim
refuses_when: nothing is held -- there is nothing to carry, and moving as if there were only walks the gripper somewhere useless
the object is already over the bin and clear of the rim -- the move is done

primitives.name: release
refuses_when: the object is not over the bin -- letting go anywhere else drops it on the floor
primitives.note: open_grip refuses while holding, on purpose: opening a loaded hand is how a grasp is lost by accident. Releasing is the same motion asked for on purpose, and it is a separate word so the accident and the intention cannot be confused.

primitives.name: insert
primitives.amplitude: how far down to press per attempt, as a fraction of the socket depth
primitives.describes: lower what is held into the socket, feeling for the jam and searching sideways when it does not go in
refuses_when: nothing is held -- there is nothing to insert
the hand is not over the socket -- pressing down anywhere else drives the object into the bench
primitives.note: The only primitive so far that expects to FAIL repeatedly and treats that as information. Everything else either works or refuses; this one presses, detects that it did not go in, backs off, shifts a millimetre and presses again. That is what makes insertion a different kind of motion rather than a tighter version of placing.

metrics.name: palm_to_object_m
metrics.sensor: range from the gripper plate to the object; a short-range rangefinder between the fingers
metrics.describes: metres from the plate between the fingers to the object's surface

metrics.name: palm_facing
metrics.sensor: the gripper's approach axis from joint angles against the face normal from vision
metrics.describes: +1 when the gripper looks straight at the face it is approaching, 0 edge-on

metrics.name: object_in_grasp_m
metrics.sensor: object position from vision, finger positions from joint encoders
metrics.describes: metres from the object to the line between the finger pads; near zero means it is INSIDE the opening

metrics.name: grip_tip_spread_m
metrics.describes: the opening between the finger pads. Opened to the object's size, then closed

metrics.name: grip_parallel
metrics.describes: +1 always. A parallel gripper cannot be anything else, which is the shape the humanoid hand had to be taught. READABLE ONLY: nothing can move it and nothing needs to

metrics.name: object_over_target_m
metrics.sensor: object position from vision, bin position known or seen
metrics.describes: horizontal distance from the object to the middle of the bin, ignoring height

metrics.name: object_above_rim_m
metrics.sensor: object position from vision, bin geometry known or seen
metrics.describes: how far the object's underside clears the bin's rim. Negative means it would strike the wall on the way across

metrics.name: object_in_target
metrics.sensor: vision, or the object ceasing to move once let go
metrics.describes: 1 when the object is inside the bin. READABLE ONLY: it is the outcome, not something to steer by

metrics.name: object_over_socket_m
metrics.sensor: grasp centre from joint encoders, socket position known a priori
metrics.describes: horizontal distance from what is held to the middle of the socket

metrics.name: insertion_depth_m
metrics.sensor: grasp centre from encoders, socket rim height known, object size estimated by the camera
metrics.describes: how far the held object's underside is BELOW the socket rim. Negative means still above it

scene.note: The task is pick AND place, so the scene has somewhere to put things. The bin stands on a riser, which is the point of it: carrying to a target at a different height is the part a lift alone does not test.

socket.note: The hard task. Same place as the bin and the same riser, so reaching it is known to work and the ONLY thing that changed is the clearance: 2 mm per side instead of 45. That is the point -- insertion is not hard because of where the hole is, it is hard because of how little room there is once you are over it, and because you do not know exactly how the object is sitting in your hand.
socket.clearance_note: Block half-extents are [0.030, 0.040, 0.030] in MuJoCo x/y/z. Socket inner half is [0.032, 0.042] laterally, so 2 mm of slack on every side, and 10 cm deep.

fridge.note: A cabinet with a hinged door and a handle, standing on the bench. The task is to open it, take out what is inside, and put that on the bench. It is here because every task so far has been about an object that was simply lying there. This one has a mechanism in it, and the door's arc is a constraint the arm has to obey rather than a path it gets to choose.

door.note: Hinged on the far side and opened by pulling the near edge toward the arm, so the door ends up as a wall off to one side and the opening faces the arm. The swing limit is what makes this articulated: the handle may travel along exactly one arc, and any pull not tangent to it is a pull the hinge refuses.

handle.note: A vertical bar on brackets, so a parallel gripper closing along its own x axis can take it from in front. It stands 82 mm off the door because the fingers are 70 mm long: at the 38 mm it started at, the jaws closed with one pad on the handle and the other 9 N deep into the door panel, holding the door SHUT while the arm pulled. A handle has to have room behind it for the hand. The brackets sit at the two ENDS of the bar, not its middle. With one central bracket the jaws closed with one pad on the bar and the other 9 N into the bracket behind it, which is a grip on the door rather than on the handle. Real handles mount at the ends for exactly this reason: the middle has to be free for a hand. The bar is 180 mm long with its brackets 164 mm apart, because the gripper plate is 80 mm tall and sits 47 mm behind the grasp centre -- so whenever the gripper holds the bar, the plate is INSIDE the bracket span. At the original 96 mm spacing that left 8 mm of margin a side, and any misalignment as the door swung jammed the plate between the brackets at 280 N, which no retreat could pull against. A handle has to have room for the whole hand, not just the fingers.

cameras.note: Four corners at one elevation, one steep overhead, and the hand. One corner view answers WHERE IS EVERYTHING, but only for the things that corner can see: the arm occludes the bench from some angles, the block hides behind the bin from others, and a single oblique view conflates sideways offset with depth -- which is why the planner reported the hand 'aligned' while it sat 4.4 cm to one side. Four corners disagree with each other, and a disagreement is information. The corners share a weakness, though, being all at the same height: none can see into an open container. The overhead camera exists for exactly that.

room.note: The FRONT-LEFT corner. Keeps the name `room` because sensing, the recorders and the dashboard all address it by that name, and renaming a camera that four files look up by string is how the bin sweep went from 12/12 to 7/12 earlier today.

segment_3.note: Already there. Sees detail, and only what the hand is pointed at.

corner_front_right.note: Opposite the original corner, across the bench.

corner_back_left.note: Behind the arm, looking back over the base toward the bin.

corner_back_right.note: The fourth corner. Sees the far side of anything the front corners see edge-on.

overhead.note: THE ONLY CAMERA THAT CAN SEE INTO THE BIN. The four corners all stand at the same height (up=1.42) around one circle, so they are four bearings on the same oblique elevation and every one of them is stopped by the bin's near wall: measured, the block vanished from all four the instant it was released into the bin, the belief froze at its last sighting, and the model spent its final eight decisions trying to re-grasp something it had already placed. This one looks down the bin's mouth at about 22 degrees off vertical -- inside the ~34 degrees the rim geometry allows -- so a placed object stays visible and placement becomes something that can be SEEN rather than read out of the simulator.

rate_limits.note: How fast each joint may move, which the range of motion does not say. Unlimited, the solvers move a FRACTION OF THE REMAINING DISTANCE each frame, so the closer they are to a large correction the harder they snap: measured, 472 deg/s at the elbow on the lift-to-carry handover, about 1.3 revolutions a second. The humanoid learned the same lesson and carries angular_rate_limits for the same reason -- a pose envelope bounds where a joint may be, never how fast it gets there, and every pose along a snap is legal.
rate_limits.reference: A collaborative arm runs 60-120 deg/s in normal operation and tops out near 180. Parallel grippers close at 50-150 mm/s.
rate_limits.finger_note: This is the APERTURE rate -- how fast the gap between the jaws changes -- which is what a gripper's datasheet quotes. Both fingers move, so each one is limited to half of it. Applying it per finger made the jaws close at 0.14 m/s, twice the declared figure, and it read on screen as the jaws snapping shut.

directed.note: The vocabulary a PLANNER works in, as opposed to the phase list a scripted controller follows. The planner never names a motion: it names a number that should become true and which controls may pursue it, and a greedy search finds the joint angles. Deciding what ought to be true is a judgement about the task; finding the pose that makes it true is a search.
directed.why_places_and_not_only_objects: The first version offered only object-relative numbers, every one of which is unreadable until something has been seen -- and the machine begins blind. The planner had nothing it could ask for, the search correctly reported that no control moved the number, and the arm sat still with its error frozen at its starting value. A vocabulary that cannot express 'go and look' cannot express this task.

goals.name: hand_y_m
goals.describes: where the hand is, in depth

goals.name: hand_pointing_down
goals.describes: how squarely the palm faces the bench, 1 for straight down. This is what replaced the pair of view_ goals: because the camera is fixed to the hand, aiming the eye and orienting the hand are the same act, and there is no reason to name them twice.

goals.name: grip_tip_spread_m
goals.describes: the gap between the pads, from the encoders

goals.name: palm_to_object_m
goals.describes: metres from the gripping surfaces to the object's surface

goals.name: object_in_grasp_m
goals.describes: metres from the object to the LINE BETWEEN THE PADS. Near zero means inside the opening, which is the condition for closing ON it rather than beside it.

goals.name: palm_facing
goals.describes: +1 looking straight at the face being approached, 0 edge-on

goals.name: object_over_target_m
goals.describes: horizontal metres from what is held to the middle of the bin

goals.name: object_above_rim_m
goals.describes: how far the held object's underside clears the rim. Negative would strike the wall.

readable_but_not_askable.name: object_in_target
readable_but_not_askable.why: the outcome. Naming it as a target is naming the goal as its own method.

readable_but_not_askable.name: holding
readable_but_not_askable.why: a state, entered by closing on something, not a number to steer

readable_but_not_askable.name: object_seen
readable_but_not_askable.why: a fact about the camera, changed by aiming it -- steer view_x_m and view_y_m instead

controls.name: arm
controls.describes: the whole arm together -- use this to put the hand or the eye somewhere

controls.name: grip
controls.describes: the jaws, one control because they are mechanically linked. Offering them separately would let a search ask for something the mechanism cannot do and then score it as an improvement.

directed.why_not_a_view_point: Looking was first offered as view_x_m/view_y_m: where the camera's axis meets the bench. It read as a place, but it was a RAY INTERSECTION, and the cheapest way to move it is to translate the camera rather than turn it. The search duly drove the hand to 8 cm above the bench with the lens still level, which scored well and saw nothing. The camera is bolted to the hand, so the honest quantity is the hand's own orientation.

sensors.note: Every instrument the machine is allowed to read. The rule has not changed -- as few as will do the job -- and these two were added because a run proved the job could not be done without them.

instruments.name: gripper_camera
instruments.mounted: on the plate, looking along the approach axis
instruments.reads: warm pixels, segmented, for where the object is across the bench
instruments.cannot_read: how far away anything is. A camera looking down a line says where along the line, never how far.

instruments.name: room_camera
instruments.mounted: fixed in the corner of the room
instruments.reads: the whole scene, for the planner to look at

instruments.name: tip_load_cells
instruments.reads: normal force at each pad, in newtons
instruments.blind_to: WHAT it is touching. A load cell reports a number, not the identity of what pressed on it, so the reading sums every contact on that pad whatever produced it.
instruments.why_added: holding was inferred from the encoders -- fingers that will not close further while being driven shut. Fingers that have stopped closing may simply have met EACH OTHER, so closing on nothing read exactly like closing on the block. The planner was told it had the block, said so in its own words, and walked down its plan with empty jaws.

instruments.name: gripper_rangefinder
instruments.mounted: beside the gripper camera, pointed along the approach axis
instruments.reads: distance to the first surface ahead, in metres
instruments.sits_on_the_centre_line: the fingers slide out to either side of it, so the beam passes between the jaws rather than into them
instruments.why_added: it answers the one question the camera cannot: HEIGHT. Without it the only way to find the bench was to open the jaws wide and close until they stalled.
